title: Ring-oscillator phase-jitter TRNG (single-RO sampled-oscillator entropy source)
topology: A free-running ring oscillator (an odd number of inverter stages, or an inverter chain closed with a NAND enable) whose output is sampled by a much slower, independent reference clock using a D flip-flop. Entropy comes from the accumulated phase jitter (thermal- and flicker-noise-driven timing uncertainty) of the fast oscillator's edges relative to the slow sampling clock: when the accumulated jitter over one sampling period spans a significant fraction of the fast oscillator's period, the sampled bit is unpredictable. A single fast RO sampled by one slow clock is the minimal baseline entropy source; the sampled bitstream is raw (biased and autocorrelated) and must be conditioned before use.
spec_class: hardware security primitive — true-random-number-generator (TRNG) noise/entropy source for cryptographic key generation, nonces, and seeding of deterministic random-bit generators (DRBGs), where the design must supply raw entropy plus a health-testable, SP 800-90B-style architecture rather than any signal-integrity or analog-precision spec

pdk_portability.notes: The sampled-ring-oscillator structure is fully digital-standard-cell portable: it needs only core inverters/NANDs and a D flip-flop, all present in sky130's standard-cell library (sky130_fd_sc_hd) and in every digital CMOS PDK. What is not portable is the raw entropy rate, which is set by the ratio of accumulated oscillator jitter to oscillator period: absolute jitter (a function of device thermal/flicker noise, supply noise, and stage count) and oscillator frequency both depend on the PDK's transistor characteristics and must be re-characterized on sky130 across corners rather than reused from another node. Entropy per output bit must be re-estimated (SP 800-90B min-entropy) on real silicon for the target PDK, never assumed from a datasheet number, because on-die deterministic coupling (supply/substrate) can masquerade as jitter and inflate an unvalidated estimate.

sizing_approach: Choose the fast ring's stage count and drive strength for a target free-running frequency high enough that many oscillator periods elapse per sampling interval (more accumulated jitter per sample); choose the sampling-clock period long relative to the oscillator period so that the standard deviation of accumulated jitter approaches or exceeds a meaningful fraction of the oscillator period, which is the condition for the sampled bit to be close to unbiased and unpredictable. The core trade-off is entropy-per-bit versus throughput: a slower sample clock accumulates more jitter (higher per-bit entropy) but lowers the raw bit rate. Baudet et al. give a stochastic model relating the entropy of the sampled bit to the jitter-variance-to-period ratio, which is the principled way to size the sampling period for a target min-entropy rather than picking it empirically. Size conservatively for the worst-case (lowest-jitter, fastest-corner) condition and rely on continuous health tests to catch entropy shortfalls, since jitter can be degraded by injection locking to nearby periodic aggressors.
layout_idioms: guard ring and a dedicated, well-decoupled supply for the ring oscillator to keep deterministic supply/substrate coupling (which is not entropy) from injection-locking the oscillator to on-chip periodic aggressors and thereby faking jitter

physical separation and orientation diversity between the entropy oscillator and any nearby clocked digital or periodic RF blocks to avoid injection locking / frequency pulling that collapses the jitter distribution
keep the sampling flip-flop close to the oscillator tap with a short, shielded route so the metastability window the design relies on is set by the flip-flop itself and not by added routing skew

provide a raw-noise-source tap (pre-conditioning) routed out to a test/debug path so the sampled entropy source can be validated per SP 800-90B on real silicon, since post-conditioning bits look random even when the raw source has failed

source.citation: M. Baudet, D. Lubicz, J. Micolod, and A. Tassiaux, "On the Security of Oscillator-Based Random Number Generators," Journal of Cryptology, vol. 24, no. 2, pp. 398-425, 2011 (IACR ePrint 2010/007 preprint publicly available). Health-testing/architecture guidance: E. Barker et al., NIST Special Publication 800-90B, "Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation," January 2018.
source.license_or_openness: Baudet et al. is cited for its stochastic jitter-entropy model and methodology only (no figures or text reproduced); an author/IACR ePrint preprint is publicly available (case 1 open-access), with the Journal of Cryptology version behind a subscription (case 2). NIST SP 800-90B is a U.S. government standard in the public domain and freely downloadable. No proprietary or NDA'd data is recorded.

notes: This single-RO sampler is the baseline every richer entropy source builds on; on its own the raw bitstream is biased and correlated and MUST be conditioned (e.g. a vetted cryptographic conditioning function or a von Neumann / XOR extractor) and continuously health-tested before the output is treated as random. Per SP 800-90B, pair it with the Repetition Count Test (RCT) and Adaptive Proportion Test (APT) as always-on health tests operating on the raw noise-source samples, and expose a raw-tap access path so the noise source can be validated independently of the conditioner. For the parallel-array evolution of this baseline that hardens entropy against a single oscillator's jitter failing, see the multi-ro-xor-entropy-source entry; for a resolution-time-based alternative see metastability-trng.
